articles.title: Cratera que 'engoliu' mãe e filha tinha 5 metros de profundidade | G1
articles.standfirst: Equipe da Secretaria de Obras de Sumaré trabalhou durante toda a tarde para fechar a galeria que se rompeu e provocou a erosão que causou a cratera que ‘engoliu’ uma mãe com a filha no colo e um homem nesta segunda-feira (16).
articles.summary: Equipe da Secretaria de Obras de Sumaré trabalhou durante toda a tarde para fechar a galeria que se rompeu e provocou a erosão que causou a cratera.
articles.body:
A cratera que se abriu em uma calçada no Centro de Sumaré (SP) e "engoliu" uma mulher com a filha de 2 anos no colo e um homem tinha cerca de 5 metros de profundidade , segundo a Secretaria Municipal de Obras.

O acidente aconteceu na manhã desta segunda-feira (16), na Avenida Rebouças, e mobilizou moradores, comerciantes e equipes de resgate. As três vítimas foram encaminhadas para a UPA Macarenko e receberam alta; a menina de 2 anos escapou ilesa .

Durante todo o período da tarde, equipes da Secretaria de Obras trabalharam no local para realizar reparos emergenciais e investigar as causas do desabamento.

De acordo com o secretário municipal de Obras, Fernando Luis Pereira, o problema estaria relacionado ao rompimento de uma estrutura subterrânea.

"A caixa de inspeção não aguentou a velocidade da água. Não é uma desculpa, mas é o que aconteceu aqui. Então ela rompeu, nós não sabíamos da existência da erosão, é claro, porque estava embaixo da terra", disse.

Segundo Pereira, foi feito um reforço da caixa de inspeção para fechar a cratera aberta.

Calçada cede e ‘engole’ mulher com criança no colo e homem em Sumaré — Foto: Circuito de segurança

A auxiliar de serviços gerais Andréia Nogueira Santos, de 38 anos, sofreu um trauma no joelho esquerdo após ser "engolida" por uma cratera . No momento do acidente, ela carregava a filha de 2 anos no colo . Apesar do susto, a menina não sofreu ferimentos e recebeu alta médica.

Andréia estava em uma padaria, na companhia do marido e da filha. O homem só não caiu no buraco pois disse que iria ao banheiro no momento em que elas deixaram o comércio .

Em nota, a prefeitura de Sumaré informou que as vítimas foram socorridas pelo Samu e encaminhadas à UPA Macarenko.

Andréia apresentou traumatismo no joelho esquerdo, sem fratura, passou por sutura, realizou exames de raio-X e recebeu medicação.

"Após avaliação médica, teve alta com orientações para repouso e continuidade do tratamento em casa".

Já a filha dela, de 2 anos, passou por avaliação pediátrica, e não apresentou sinais de traumatismo ou outras alterações clínicas e também recebeu alta médica.

O representante comercial Adrian Baldisera, de 25 anos, ainda tenta entender o que aconteceu nesta segunda.

"Eu estava voltando para o meu carro. Do nada, estava lá dentro do buraco" , disse Adrian, que havia parado para entregar medicamentos em uma farmácia próxima ao local do acidente.

Segundo ele, o proprietário do estabelecimento não estava presente e, ao retornar para o veículo, foi surpreendido pelo desabamento.

Apesar da rapidez da ocorrência, Adrian contou que teve tempo para um pensamento durante a queda.

"Deu até tempo de pensar. O único flash que eu tenho é: 'caramba, qual o fundo desse negócio aqui?'"

Adrian contou que sofreu um corte na cabeça, precisou levar cinco pontos e afirma que as dores começaram a aparecer somente após o susto inicial.

"Agora que a adrenalina está baixando, está começando a aparecer dor. Estou sentindo nos joelhos também."

Adrian Baldisera, de 25 anos, foi engolido por uma cratera que se abriu na calçada em Sumaré (SP) nesta segunda-feira (16) e levou cinco pontos na cabeça — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

Após receber atendimento, o representante comercial afirmou que pretende reunir documentos, imagens e registros do acidente para buscar responsabilização judicial.

"Agora eu vou procurar um advogado e vou entrar na justiça contra a prefeitura. Isso daí é uma coisa inacreditável, cara. Assim, tava uma casquinha de calçada", reclamou.

O afundamento provocou alterações no trânsito da Avenida da Amizade. O trecho próximo à cratera foi isolado e os motoristas precisaram utilizar um desvio durante os trabalhos das equipes.

A Secretaria Municipal de Mobilidade Urbana e Rural (SMMUR) acompanhou a circulação de veículos e orientou os motoristas durante a interdição.

Mulher com criança no colo e homem caem após abertura de buraco em Sumaré — Foto: Câmeras de segurança

articles.title: Brasil e Espanha defendem o multilateralismo e a necessidade de reformas na ONU  | G1
articles.standfirst: Nesta segunda-feira (16), o presidente Lula foi recebido no Palácio de La Moncloa pelo primeiro-ministro espanhol, Pedro Sánchez.
articles.summary: Nesta segunda-feira (16), o presidente Lula foi recebido no Palácio de La Moncloa pelo primeiro-ministro espanhol, Pedro Sánchez.
articles.body:
O presidente Lula chega na noite desta segunda-feira (16) em Brasília, depois de uma viagem à Turquia e às Filipinas . O último compromisso foi nesta segunda-feira (16) cedo, na Espanha .

No fim da manhã, o presidente Lula foi recebido no Palácio de La Moncloa pelo primeiro-ministro espanhol, Pedro Sánchez . Eles tiveram um encontro a sós e, depois, participaram de uma reunião estendida, com ministros dos dois países.

Brasil e Espanha defendem o multilateralismo e a necessidade de reformas na ONU — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

A visita à Espanha não estava no cronograma original da viagem do presidente Lula, que na semana passada participou da COP31, na Turquia, e da reunião de cúpula da Associação das Nações do Sudeste Asiático, nas Filipinas.

O Brasil e a Espanha divulgaram notas sobre o encontro. Afirmaram que Lula e Sánchez defenderam o multilateralismo e a necessidade de reformas na ONU. Segundo o governo espanhol, Sanchez destacou a importância das instituições democráticas e da coesão social diante da ameaça da extrema direita.

O encontro entre Lula e Pedro Sánchez aconteceu a menos de duas semanas das eleições parlamentares na Espanha. O primeiro-ministro antecipou a votação depois que projetos do governo para enfrentar a crise de moradia foram derrubados pelo Parlamento. A Espanha enfrenta uma onda de protestos contra o alto custo de vida, especialmente dos aluguéis.

articles.title: US government is proposing one sentence change in USCIS rules that would change every H-1B visa extension form, with thousands losing their approval
articles.summary: The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has proposed a change to immigration rules that could make it harder for thousands of foreign workers to get
articles.body: The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has proposed a change to immigration rules that could make it harder for thousands of foreign workers to get their visa extensions approved. The change, one sentence long, would end a rule that requires US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to give weight to its own earlier approval when reviewing an extension request. The change could affect H-1B, L-1, O-1, TN, E and other work visa categories. According to immigration law firm Reddy Neumann Brown PC, the proposal is titled “Removing Deference to Prior USCIS Determinations of Eligibility”. It was published on October 14, 2026. Public comments were due on November 13, 2026.What is the proposed USCIS change Under the current rule, USCIS generally gives deference to an earlier approval when an employer files an extension for the same worker, job and underlying circumstances. This means the immigration officer usually relies on the previous decision unless there is a major error, a change in circumstances or new information that affects the worker’s eligibility.DHS now wants to remove this requirement by deleting Section 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5) from the rules.If the proposal becomes final, USCIS officers could review an extension application from the beginning, even if the same employer and worker have already received approval for the same job. Officers would still be allowed to consider the previous approval, but they would no longer be required to give it special weight.It must be noted that the change does not mean that all existing visa approvals will be cancelled. Instead, it could make future extension applications more difficult and increase the chances of additional questions or requests for evidence.How many visa petitions could be affectedDHS estimates that around 208,429 petitions filed each year could lose the benefit of deference to earlier approvals. H-1B petitions account for more than 75% of Form I-129 filings, according to the information cited by Reddy Neumann Brown PC. This means H-1B workers are likely to be among the most affected.The impact could be particularly significant for Indian professionals. According to USCIS data cited by the law firm, Indian-born workers accounted for 77.6% of H-1B approvals for continuing employment in fiscal year 2025.Will H-1B workers lose their visa extensionsThe proposed rule does not automatically mean that thousands of workers will lose their approvals. However, it could lead to more extension applications being questioned. USCIS officers could reopen issues that were already reviewed in an earlier application, such as whether a job qualifies as a specialty occupation or whether a worker meets the requirements for the position.DHS estimates that the change could result in around 6,044 additional requests for evidence (RFEs) every year. An RFE asks an employer or applicant to provide more information before USCIS makes a decision.The law firm also noted that DHS’s own analysis found no statistically significant difference in denial rates between periods when deference was applied and when it was not. The measurable impact was an increase in RFEs.How could the change affect workersMore RFEs could lead to longer processing times for visa extensions. This could create uncertainty for workers whose employment depends on receiving an approval before their current status expires.H-1B workers who file an extension on time can generally continue working for the same employer for up to 240 days after their I-94 period expires while the application is pending. Longer processing times could push more cases closer to this limit.The proposal could also affect international travel. Some workers wait for their extension approval before travelling abroad to obtain a new visa stamp. Delays could force them to postpone trips, including travel for family emergencies.Small businesses could face additional challenges as well. DHS data cited by the law firm shows that 57% of employers classified as small entities that filed H-1B extensions in fiscal year 2025 were small businesses. The median small employer filed just one petition.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? Find out in the TOI AI Masterclass.

articles.title: Jake Gyllenhaal has joined a 10th annual US celebrity auction supporting custom homes for injured veterans; the charity has built more than 400 homes and bidding runs through November 20, 2026
articles.summary: Jake Gyllenhaal has joined the 10th annual Veterans Day Celebrity Auction hosted by Homes For Our Troops, the national nonprofit that builds specially
articles.body: Jake Gyllenhaal has joined the 10th annual Veterans Day Celebrity Auction hosted by Homes For Our Troops, the national nonprofit that builds specially adapted custom homes for severely injured post 9/11 veterans. According to the charity’s announcement and its Building Homes programme, the online auction opened on November 10 and will close on November 20, 2026, with every winning bid supporting homes designed to restore independence for injured veterans and their families.The auction is headlined by longtime supporters Jake Tapper and George Clooney, but its celebrity lineup extends well beyond them. Gyllenhaal appears alongside stars including Adam Sandler, Jennifer Aniston, Ben Stiller, Dave Chappelle, Jerry Seinfeld, Jon Bon Jovi, Paul Rudd, and Sarah Silverman, offering fans a chance to bid on experiences and memorabilia while supporting a practical cause. Read more details about it, as per the reports, here:What Gyllenhaal joinedGyllenhaal’s participation places him among dozens of entertainers, athletes, and public figures contributing to the milestone auction. The event gives supporters access to celebrity experiences, behind the scenes opportunities, meet and greets, and one of a kind collectibles.For bidders, the appeal is not only the chance to connect with a favourite star. Each winning bid helps fund Homes For Our Troops’ work building and donating mortgage free, specially adapted homes for veterans whose injuries make ordinary housing difficult to navigate. The organisation says its homes include more than 40 major adaptations, such as wider hallways and doorways, automatic door openers, generators, safe rooms, roll under sinks and counters, and pull down shelving. These features are intended to help veterans live more independently at home.A decade of celebrity supportThis year marks the 10th annual Veterans Day Celebrity Auction, a milestone for an event that has become a recurring part of the charity’s fundraising calendar. CNN anchor Jake Tapper, a national board ambassador for Homes For Our Troops, has helped organise and promote the auction for a decade. Tapper said the event matters because every bid and donation helps build homes that give severely injured veterans greater freedom and independence. His continued involvement has helped bring together celebrities, donors, and veterans around a cause that extends beyond a single fundraising night.George Clooney, another longtime supporter, returns as a headline host. He described the charity’s work as helping veterans and their families live more independently by creating homes adapted to the challenges they face.How the auction worksThe online auction is hosted through eBay for Charity at eBay.com/hfot. Bidding opened on November 10 at 4 p.m. Pacific Time, or 7 p.m. Eastern Time, and is scheduled to close on November 20 at the same time. The 10 day format gives supporters time to browse the offerings, place bids, and follow the competition. The auction includes a broad mix of experiences and collectibles, making it accessible to fans with different interests and budgets.Every dollar raised through winning bids supports the charity’s broader mission. Homes For Our Troops builds homes where veterans choose to live and continues its relationship with them after delivery, helping them rebuild their lives beyond the initial construction project.Why the homes matterHomes For Our Troops was founded in 2004 and has since built more than 400 specially adapted homes nationwide. The organisation says more than 90 veterans are currently on its active project list, with a long term goal of building a home for every veteran who qualifies for one.The homes are designed for veterans with severe injuries, including multiple limb amputations, partial or full paralysis, blindness, severe burns, and severe traumatic brain injury. By removing physical barriers and creating accessible living spaces, the charity aims to help veterans regain some of the independence they lost through service.The organisation says that a mortgage free, adapted home allows veterans to focus on recovery, family, education, and new careers. Many recipients have gone on to become advocates, speakers, and community leaders, using their experiences to raise awareness about veteran suicide, homelessness, and post traumatic stress disorder.A fundraising model with reachThe celebrity auction works because it turns fan enthusiasm into direct support for a tangible outcome. A bidder may be drawn by the chance to meet a star or own a collectible, but the money raised goes toward something practical: a home built around a veteran’s specific needs.Homes For Our Troops says nearly 90 cents of every dollar it spends goes directly to programme services supporting veterans. The charity is privately funded and relies heavily on individual donors and community fundraisers, alongside corporate and foundation support.The 10th anniversary auction also reflects how celebrity involvement can sustain attention for a cause over time. Rather than treating veteran support as a one time event, the charity has built a recurring tradition that brings new supporters into its work each year.What bidders can do nowWith bidding open through November 20, supporters have a limited window to participate. They can visit the auction page, review the available experiences and memorabilia, and place bids knowing that the proceeds support Homes For Our Troops’ home building mission.For those who cannot bid, the charity’s work continues beyond the auction. Its website outlines how donations support the construction of accessible homes and how the organisation works with veterans after they move in.Gyllenhaal’s involvement adds another familiar name to an effort that has already helped more than 400 veterans receive specially adapted homes. As the auction enters its final days, the focus remains on turning celebrity attention into lasting independence for the people the charity serves.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.summary: GURDASPUR: The killing of a Punjab Police head constable, whose bullet-riddled body was found on the roadside near Manakour bypass, has raised fresh
articles.body: GURDASPUR: The killing of a Punjab Police head constable, whose bullet-riddled body was found on the roadside near Manakour bypass, has raised fresh concerns over the safety of police personnel in the state's border districts. This is the fifth killing of a policeman in Punjab since February.Taking serious note of the incident, special director general of police (Law and Order) Parveen Kumar Sinha arrived in Gurdaspur on Monday to take stock of the situation and supervise the investigation. He also attended the cremation of head constable Vinod Kumar.Sinha and inspector general of police, Border Range, Gurpreet Singh Bhullar, shouldered the bier.Speaking to TOI, Sinha said preliminary indications suggested that it was a targeted attack on a policeman. “He died of a bullet injury. We are investigating all aspects of the case,” he said.Asked about the preliminary findings of the investigation, Sinha said the last available evidence with the police indicated that Vinod had taken a lift on a motorcycle from two persons whose faces were muffled. Investigators are examining the circumstances in which he came in contact with the two men and what happened thereafter.According to reports, Vinod, a wireless operator posted at Sujanpur police station in Pathankot, was a resident of Krishna Nagar in Gurdaspur. Following his promotion, he had gone to the Police Training Centre at Jahan Khelan and was subsequently sent to Sangrur for training. He was returning from Sangrur on November 15 when he was killed.Meanwhile, a CCTV footage shared by SAD leader Bikram Singh Majithia on X purportedly shows two masked men abducting Vinod and shooting him. Majithia alleged that the head constable was kidnapped and murdered. The footage and the circumstances depicted in it have not been independently verified.“Guru Dokhi Bhagwant, criminals are openly shooting police personnel in the border areas. How are they operating with such impunity while you remain obsessed with 'tari wale baingan'? Is this your idea of law and order?”, he wrote.The killing has also reportedly been claimed by an outfit called Tariq-e-Taliban Hindustan in a social media post, which attributed the attack to its operatives under what it called “Operation Noor”. The post also threatened further attacks on security personnel. articles.body: Three of the world's most powerful leaders are set to meet for the first-ever trilateral summit between the United States, China and Russia.US President Donald Trump has outlined the agenda for his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, saying the discussions will cover denuclearisation, Iran, the Ukraine war, economics and trade.Speaking to reporters, Trump said the three leaders would discuss denuclearisation, adding that the issue would be part of the agenda. "We're going to be talking about denuclearisation," he said, according to ANI.The proposed discussion comes after the expiry of the New START treaty between the US and Russia in February 2026. The agreement had placed limits on the strategic nuclear arsenals of the two countries. China has so far resisted joining nuclear arms control negotiations with Washington and Moscow.Iran is another issue Trump wants to raise during the meeting. "We'll talk about Iran," he said.Both China and Russia maintain strategic ties with Tehran. China is a major buyer of Iranian oil, while Russia has maintained military and diplomatic cooperation with Iran.The discussion could cover the ongoing conflict involving Iran and the role Beijing and Moscow could play in addressing regional tensions.Ukraine is another key issue Trump wants to discuss with Xi and Putin. Calling it his "favourite subject", Trump said, "Ukraine is losing. Ukraine and Russia are losing 25,000 souls per month, so we'll be talking about that."His remarks come amid continuing efforts to negotiate an end to the war. The inclusion of Ukraine is also notable as US officials had earlier indicated that the conflict would not be part of the trilateral discussions. Trump has now said he intends to raise the issue with both leaders.Trump also said economics and trade would feature in the discussions, without specifying the issues he intends to raise.The US and China continue to face trade disagreements over tariffs, technology and critical minerals. Russia's economic ties with China have also expanded since western sanctions were imposed on Moscow following its invasion of Ukraine.The trilateral meeting is scheduled for November 19 in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. articles.title: A California woman sold her $350,000 home after an AI scammer posing as ‘General Hospital’ star Steve Burton convinced her they were in love and would build a future together
articles.summary: A woman in Southern California lost her life savings and sold her home after becoming convinced that General Hospital actor Steve Burton was in love with
articles.body: A woman in Southern California lost her life savings and sold her home after becoming convinced that General Hospital actor Steve Burton was in love with her. The deception involved AI-generated videos and messages that made an impersonator appear and sound like the television star. According to ABC7 Chicago, the woman’s family discovered the scam only after substantial sums had disappeared. What began as an online conversation developed into a financial disaster, leaving her facing debt, possible bankruptcy and an uncertain future.How an AI romance scam using Steve Burton's identity beganThe victim, Abigail Ruvalcaba, began receiving messages on Facebook Messenger in October 2024 from someone claiming to be Steve Burton, the actor who portrays Jason Morgan on General Hospital. ABC7 Chicago said the impersonator sent videos that looked like Burton talking directly to Abigail and telling her he loved her.The videos were convincing enough to convince her she was talking to the real actor. AI had been used to recreate Burton’s look and voice, so it sounded as if the celebrity was speaking to her personally.The conversation eventually moved from Facebook Messenger to WhatsApp. According to Fox News, Abigail was encouraged to believe that the relationship was genuine and that the two could build a future together.The scammer reportedly discussed marriage and a shared life, making the relationship appear more personal than an ordinary exchange between a celebrity and a fan.The impersonator used money troubles to deepen the deceptionThe scam became more damaging when the impersonator claimed to have lost property during the Los Angeles wildfires. According to ABC7 Chicago, Abigail was told that Burton needed financial help and that the couple would eventually purchase a home together.The story gave the requests for money an apparent explanation. Instead of seeing the payments as suspicious, Abigail believed she was helping someone she loved through a difficult period.She sent at least $81,304 in gift cards, cash and Bitcoin, according to a Los Angeles Police Department incident report. The transfers drained her savings and left her in serious financial trouble.Fox News later described how the scam continued even after her available money had been exhausted. The impersonator encouraged Abigail to sell her condominium, presenting the decision as a way for them to begin a new life together.How did the scam lead to a home saleAbigail eventually sold her condominium in Harbor City, California, for $350,000. ABC7 Chicago reported that she had initially resisted the idea but later agreed after continued encouragement from the person she believed was Burton.The property sale represented a significant turning point. The condominium had been part of her family's financial security, but the impersonator persuaded her that selling it would help fulfil their supposed plans.According to Fox News, Abigail's daughter Vivian said the property was sold for considerably less than comparable homes in the neighbourhood. The quick transaction also meant that the family had little opportunity to intervene before the sale went through.The impersonator was expected to receive another $70,000 from the proceeds. However, Vivian discovered what was happening before that transfer could be completed and stopped it.KTLA reported that the family was left struggling to protect the property after the transaction. The condominium had subsequently been transferred to new owners, complicating efforts to recover it.Steve Burton confirmed the videos were fakeThe real Steve Burton was shown one of the videos used in the scam by ABC7 Chicago. The actor said the voice sounded exactly like his own, confirming why Abigail had struggled to recognise the deception.Burton also said that he knew of hundreds of people who had lost money to scammers pretending to be him. He said impostors often approached fans through comments on his verified Instagram account before directing them towards other profiles where money was requested.The actor made his position clear, saying he did not need fans' money and would never ask them for it. He also described meeting people at public appearances who believed they had maintained online relationships with him for years, only to discover that he did not know them.The family is fighting to recover the propertyAbigail's daughter Vivian stepped in after discovering the extent of the deception. According to ABC7 Chicago, she holds power of attorney for her mother and decided to speak publicly about the case to warn other families about the dangers of AI impersonation.The family has filed a lawsuit seeking to reverse the condominium sale. Their lawyer argues that Abigail was unable to distinguish between reality and the fabricated relationship, raising questions about whether she had the mental capacity to enter into the property contract.But the legal fight is being fought. The attorney for the buyers of the property told ABC7 Chicago that the claim that Abigail was unable to contract was not true and that the evidence was in their favor. It'll all be settled in court.The family hopes that sharing Abigail's story will make others more cautious about strangers claiming to be celebrities online.You use AI every day. articles.title: Saudi Arabia dismisses commander of coalition forces fighting Houthis
articles.summary: Move comes as government forces withdraw from Red Sea coast to halt Houthi approach to interim capital Aden.
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia has replaced the commander overseeing its coalition forces as they battle the Iranian-backed Houthis in Yemen.

King Salman issued a decree on Monday assigning General Fayyad al-Ruwaili to the command, according to Saudi state media. The removal of Lieutenant General Fahd bin Hamad al-Salman came as coalition forces were forced to abandon their recent push to recapture regions along the Red Sea coast in order to reinforce the Yemeni government’s interim capital, Aden.

Al-Salman was appointed as a military adviser to the Saudi defence minister a day after coalition forces were forced to withdraw.

Yemen’s internationally recognised government said on Sunday that coalition forces were withdrawing from areas near the key Bab al-Mandeb strait – via which Saudi oil exports have been flowing while the United States-Iran war stifles traffic through the Strait of Hormuz – to focus on defending Aden.

The retreat marked a major setback for the Saudi-backed campaign against the Houthis, who have been firing ballistic missiles at Saudi Arabia’s airports and oil facilities since Yemen’s civil war restarted in July.

A Houthi offensive in September saw the government lose control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including the key port city of Mocha . Later Houthi advances also saw Taiz completely besieged by the Houthis.

Government forces – backed by the Saudi-led coalition – quickly retook key positions near Bab al-Mandeb after the Houthi advance on the strait and the Red Sea coast this summer, but have been unable to retake Mocha.

They have said they killed or wounded 173 Houthi fighters as part of Operation Dawn of Yemen and engaged the Houthis in Marib, Lahij and in al-Jawf.

However, they are now retreating from theterritory they held near the Bab al-Mandeb strait and preparing to fortify defences around Aden, after the Houthis advanced to an area 60 kilometres (37 miles) north of the city.

Yemeni Armed Forces spokesperson Majed al-Nuzaili defended the retreat, saying it was part of a wider tactical manoeuvre.

“[The redeployment] is an extension of the heroic positions of the popular resistance and the southern forces in protecting the temporary capital Aden,” he said on X.

As the fighting continues, civilians remain exposed. Houthi-affiliated media reported coalition air strikes on the capital Sanaa, which the Iran-backed group took in 2014, and said one person was killed in an attack on a school in Taiz.

Authorities in the besieged city of Taiz have called for humanitarian corridors to allow civilians to evacuate, as medical officials warned hospitals could be forced to end operations within two days due to a lack of fuel and oxygen.

Earlier on Monday, Saudi Arabia said it had shot down two Houthi drones targeting the Mecca and Riyadh regions.

articles.title: Canada could turn to Chinese automakers without US deal: Carney
articles.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Monday that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers to shore up its struggling auto industry if trade negotiations with the Trump administration fail to produce a deal. Speaking to reporters in Cambodia, Carney said he remains focused on reaching an agreement with the U.S. but warned that Canada would…
articles.body:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Monday that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers to shore up its struggling auto industry if trade negotiations with the Trump administration fail to produce a deal.

Speaking to reporters in Cambodia, Carney said he remains focused on reaching an agreement with the U.S. but warned that Canada would seek other partners if the trade policies continue to undermine the two countries’ longstanding manufacturing relationship.

“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters. “That market has become less integrated because of U.S. trade actions.”

He suggested that Canada could pursue investment from automakers in China, Europe or Japan if negotiations with the U.S. fail to secure the future of its auto industry.

Asked whether the prospect of Chinese investment was meant to give Canada an advantage in negotiations with Washington, Carney responded, “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction.”

“If they’re not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said of Canada’s auto industry workers and manufacturing facilities. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”

His comments come ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in China later this week, with automanufacturing expected to be among the topics discussed.

The two countries struck a trade deal in January that reduced Canadian tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles from 100 percent to 6.1 percent, allowing up to 49,000 vehicles into the country annually. China, in return, agreed to ease tariffs on Canadian agricultural exports, including canola.

President Trump, however, threatened a 100 percent tariff on Canada if it were to make a deal with China. Carney subsequently clarified that Canada was not seeking a broader free trade agreement with China.

Trump’s tariffs have placed mounting pressure on Canada’s auto industry, which relies on closely connected manufacturing operations across the U.S., Canada and Mexico. Major automakers, including Ford, General Motors and Stellantis, operate factories in all three countries, with parts frequently crossing borders multiple times before vehicles are completed.

articles.title: Microsoft asked him to go back to India after his  H-1B visa was rejected. Kunal Bahl returned, but to build Snapdeal, Titan Capital
articles.summary: An H-1B visa rejection in 2007 changed the course of entrepreneur Kunal Bahl's career.
articles.body: An H-1B visa rejection in 2007 changed the course of entrepreneur Kunal Bahl's career. He was working at Microsoft in the United States and was asked to relocate to the company's India office after his work visa petition was rejected. Instead of waiting another year to reapply, Bahl decided to return to India and build his own business. Nearly two decades later, Bahl is the co-founder of e-commerce platform Snapdeal and investment firm Titan Capital. He is also a judge on Shark Tank India and has helped build two publicly listed companies.Recalling the experience in an interview with Business Insider, Bahl said the visa rejection was a blessing in disguise."Entrepreneurship was always on the cards for me. An H-1B rejection just fast-tracked it," he said.Microsoft asked Kunal Bahl to move to India after H-1B rejectionBahl had graduated from the University of Pennsylvania, where he pursued a programme combining engineering and business. He joined Microsoft as a full-time employee in October 2006 after completing an internship with the company. But as fate would have it, his H-1B petition was rejected in June or July 2007, when he was approaching the end of his temporary work authorisation in the US.The decision came as a surprise to him, particularly because he was employed by one of the world's biggest technology companies. Microsoft offered him the option of relocating to its India office and trying for an H-1B visa again after 12 months.But Bahl decided against continuing his corporate career in India while waiting for another visa opportunity."I no longer had the baggage of having to figure out this H-1B situation. I felt liberated because I didn't have to worry about visas or Green Cards," he recalled. By that time, he had already been thinking about entrepreneurship and decided that if he returned to India, he would work for himself rather than continue working for Microsoft.How H-1B rejection led to SnapdealBahl contacted his high-school friend Rohit Bansal, who was then working at a financial institution, and asked whether he wanted to start a business together. The two had discussed entrepreneurship while studying together and quickly agreed to pursue the idea.Their company was incorporated on September 12, 2007, a few days before Bahl arrived in India.The founders pooled approximately $60,000 from their personal savings to get the business started. They initially launched a physical coupon-book business before moving to online couponing and eventually building Snapdeal into one of India's early e-commerce platforms.Bahl said starting a company in India in 2007 was challenging. Internet penetration and smartphone adoption were limited, digital payments were not widespread, and raising money from angel investors was difficult.The two entrepreneurs initially worked out of a small office in the basement of a residential building in Delhi's furniture market. They also stayed with their families to save on accommodation and food expenses.Their business eventually grew into Snapdeal, which became a major name in India's online shopping market.From Snapdeal to Titan Capital and Shark Tank IndiaBahl and Bansal expanded their entrepreneurial journey into startup investing in 2011 by establishing Titan Capital.Over the past 15 years, the investment firm has backed more than 320 startups, according to Bahl's Business Insider interview. Its investments include companies such as Ola and Urban Company.The founders also went on to build businesses that eventually became two publicly listed companies.Bahl is now associated with AceVector, the parent company of Snapdeal, Unicommerce and Stellaro Brands. He is also a judge on Shark Tank India, where entrepreneurs pitch their businesses to investors.'No better time to come back to India'Looking back, Bahl described his H-1B rejection as a fortunate turning point, although he acknowledged that the experience was painful at the time. "In hindsight, my not getting the H-1B visa was serendipitous," he said, adding that it became part of a larger journey that brought him back to India to help build the country's startup ecosystem. But he admitted that returning to India is not an equally easy decision for everyone facing immigration difficulties in the US. It was easier for him to pack his bags and leave as he was unmarried.India now has widespread internet and smartphone access, a larger pool of skilled professionals, more coworking spaces, a stronger funding ecosystem and greater government support for startups. "There is no better time to come back," he said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Scores of Bahraini Shiite clerics get life in jail, accused of plotting with Iran
articles.summary: Scores of Bahrainis, mostly Shiite Muslim clerics according to a rights group, have been sentenced to life in prison on charges of colluding with Iran’s Revolutionary Guards to undermine the state, prosecutors said on Monday.
articles.body: Scores of Bahrainis, mostly Shiite Muslim clerics according to a rights group, have been sentenced to life in prison on charges of colluding with Iran’s Revolutionary Guards to undermine the state, prosecutors said on Monday. Bahrain, a Shiite-majority country ruled by a Sunni Muslim family and home to the U.S. Navy’s Fifth Fleet, has long been anxious about Iranian influence. After Tehran began attacking Bahrain this year in response to the US-Israeli war on Iran, Bahrain accused it of fostering sedition, and launched a crackdown on Shiite clerics. Between May and June, authorities arrested more than 50 clerics and religious orators, accusing them of trying to incite rebellion and overthrow the ruling order with help from Iran’s dominant Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Reuters reported this month. The Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy (BIRD) said 64 defendants had been sentenced to life and five others to 15 years in prison after a trial that activists said began on July 5. It said 60 of the defendants were Shiite clerics. A person close to the clerics’ defense teams described the verdicts as “worse than anything we imagined,” noting that not a single defendant had been acquitted. The person spoke on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter. Bahrain’s top Shiite cleric sentenced to life Some Shiites say they are oppressed for their beliefs, and in the early 2010s, the government jailed hundreds of mostly Shiite anti-government protesters. Iran has rejected accusations of interference in Bahrain‘s internal affairs, but this year’s regional war has put authorities on edge once more. “We are confronting an ideology that demands obedience to Iran’s leadership above Bahrain‘s sovereign authority,” Lieutenant General Tariq Al Hassan, head of Bahrain‘s Public Security Agency, said this month. The High Criminal Court convicted all the defendants, some of whom were tried in absentia, of establishing and running a terrorist group linked to the IRGC that sought to overthrow the government, the prosecution said. It did not specify the number of defendants or identify them as clerics or members of a particular sect, but accused them of raising funds without authorization and using mosques, religious sermons and charitable and educational institutions to promote allegiance to Iran’s supreme leader. Some defendants were fined 100,000 Bahraini dinars ($265,000), and the court ordered the confiscation of more than 8 million Bahraini dinars ($21 million) for charitable purposes. Among those sentenced to life imprisonment was Sheikh Isa Qassim, according to BIRD, who is widely regarded as the spiritual leader of Bahrain‘s Shiite community and has lived in Iran since 2018. “To sentence a man in his late 80s, knowing that the conviction has no practical effect, is difficult to see as anything other than an act of retaliation,” said Sayed Ahmed Alwadaei, BIRD’s director of advocacy. Rights groups question fairness of trial Bahrain stripped Qassim of his citizenship in 2016, accusing him of promoting sectarianism, serving foreign interests and undermining loyalty to the state. The decision sparked protests and drew criticism from human rights groups and the US. BIRD condemned the latest verdicts, citing allegations of torture, coerced confessions and restrictions on access to evidence. It said defendants had been interrogated without lawyers and pressured into signing statements they had not read. Twenty rights groups, including Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, had previously raised concerns about the proceedings, citing allegations of torture, incommunicado detention and restrictions on access to evidence. “This prosecution has torn religious leaders from their congregations and left families living under threats, fear and uncertainty,” said BIRD’s Alwadaei. The prosecution said defendants’ legal rights had been upheld, with lawyers present and opportunities to examine evidence and question witnesses.

articles.title: United Airlines says it has resolved a ‘widespread system outage’
articles.summary: United Airlines on Monday said a widespread system outage that delayed flight departures is over.
articles.body: United Airlines on Monday said a widespread system outage that delayed flight departures is over. In a statement early Monday evening, the airline said it had resolved a technology issue linked to the problem, which came on the heels of a nationwide FAA ground stop. While some flights were delayed, the company said, there was no impact on flights in progress or on United Express flights. United announced the outage roughly an hour earlier, just before 5 p.m. The union representing United pilots said in a statement that the outage had affected multiple pilot-facing applications, including crew communications and messaging systems, as well as the airline’s ability to provide final aircraft weight information for departing flights. The union said it was working with management to better understand the scope of the disruption. Pilots had been advised to follow procedures in the flight operations manual, according to the statement. A passenger on a United flight bound for Hong Kong told NBC News that a pilot announced that they’d been unable to get performance data for takeoff because of an IT issue. The pilot said they planned on doing “old school” calculations so they could take off, according to the passenger, Halina Eth. In another announcement, the pilot said that systems were back online and there was a “very narrow window of opportunity to get this flight in the air,” according to a video shared with NBC News. The issue did not appear to be related to technical issues that prompted the ground stop that halted air travel across the United States for more than four hours Friday evening. Other airlines did not appear to be affected by Monday’s United issue. It’s the latest system relied on by millions of Americans to falter. Earlier Monday, JPMorganChase said a technical issue was causing some banking transactions to be delayed for both its own customers and others. Late Friday, the FAA was forced to issue a nationwide ground stop after a fiber upgrade crashed a critical communication system. By Monday, air travel in the U.S. was largely returning to normal after a chaotic weekend for travelers, crews and airlines. And last week, Microsoft Outlook went down due to what the tech giant said was a “bug” and overwhelmed servers. While there is no evidence that any of the issues are related, they seem to be fulfilling concerns about America’s overreliance on aging infrastructure. They’re also occurring against a backdrop of warnings about AI risks and cyberattacks, stoking fears that wider problems may be afoot.

articles.title: Children dropping out of school: What can politicians do about it?
articles.summary: The government believes around a third of young people who are persistently absent in Years 10 and 11 in England go on to be not in education, employment or training.
articles.body:
The stories of Eva and Mali - which you can watch in the video above - and the many teenagers like them who don't go to school, either regularly or at all, strike to the heart of one of the many big challenges the Milburn Review is seeking to address.

The government-commissioned work, led by former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn, is looking into how to solve the problem of nearly one million young people not being in employment, education or training, or Neet.

A key challenge is addressing the issue of school absence.

The government believes around a third of young people who are persistently absent in Years 10 and 11 in England go on to be Neet, compared with 10% of those who are not persistently absent.

Persistent absence almost doubles between Years 7 and 9, reaching around one in four children by Year 9.

Thirteen-year-old Eva hadn't been to school for 15 months before September.

She described how she used to get up every morning, try to get ready for school and get stuck by the front door.

Mali, 18, stopped attending school three years ago when she was in year 10.

We shared their stories with the decision makers and those who want to be our decision makers – in other words, those in government and those who would like to be.

It offers an insight into the political arguments to come.

Labour reckons the Conservatives' education reforms of the last decade and a half served academic high achievers very well but created what one source described as an an "endless treadmill of failure" for some - and so let them down.

A government spokesperson said: "When children feel they belong at school, they show up, and when they show up, they achieve."

Therefore, the spokesperson added, "the education secretary is driving ambitious reforms to boost attendance" and "intervene earlier when children need support".

The Liberal Democrats also sought to pin the blame on the Tories.

Munira Wilson, who speaks for the party on education, said "the Conservatives failed to give them the support they needed after lockdown, and years of underinvestment in their recovery are now showing up in rising mental health figures". She added that "every young person should feel they belong".

These reactions prompt some of the big questions that arise from Eva and Mali's experiences.

Where should responsibility for their situations lie? The individual, the parents, the rules in the pandemic, schools, colleges, mental health provision?

Perhaps a combination of all of these things in some instances and other things besides.

The Conservatives have pushed back strongly against the criticism from Labour and the Liberal Democrats.

Shadow education secretary Laura Trott told the BBC: "We mustn't give up on any child, every day a child misses school sets them back.

"Schools are doing great work to bring absence down. Those children who have special education needs or are struggling to leave home, need specialist support and in some cases specialist schools."

And she added: "High academic standards lift everyone up. It is insulting to suggest that not all children are capable of good academic outcomes. Too much maths and English are not making young people Neet."

Former Conservative cabinet minister Suella Braverman, now Reform UK's education spokesperson, told us: "As someone who co-founded and chaired an outstanding state school with a high proportion of children on free school meals but a below average school absence rate, it is clear that the culture and teaching in a school can make a huge difference."

She added that "greater parental engagement" and a "culture of perseverance" were essential too.

The government is expected to accept the broad thrust of Alan Milburn's report, before responding in detail in the next month or so.

We are told there will be an announcement from Education Secretary Lucy Powell directly relevant to Eva, Mali and the many like them, later this week.

articles.title: 'Strangers walked into my Travelodge hotel room while I was in towel'
articles.summary: Jade said she is concerned her experience shows not enough has been done regarding safety issues at the hotel chain.
articles.body:
Jade Clarke was undressed and brushing her teeth when two strangers walked into her hotel room last month.

The 35-year-old was getting ready for a wedding at a Travelodge in Glasgow when the incident happened, leaving her and the accidental intruders "mortified".

It is the latest in a series of similar incidents at the hotel chain, with a report finding there were room intrusions at almost one in 10 Travelodges this summer.

Travelodge apologised and said it had conducted an investigation and taken steps to ensure it did not happen again.

The interim chief executive of the firm has said "nobody is working harder on room security than we are today".

But Jade, who lives in Edinburgh, got in touch with BBC Scotland via Your Voice to share her experience.

She said: "My experience is showing that incidents like this are still happening and people's privacy, their security and their safety are still potentially being put at risk, which isn't OK."

Jade had travelled to the Queen Street Travelodge in Glasgow on 29 October, the night before her friend's wedding, so she could take her time getting ready.

She said she did her hair and make up and was brushing her teeth before getting dressed when she heard the hotel room door open and close.

She grabbed a towel to cover herself and put her head round the door into the corridor to investigate, when she was met with a couple and their suitcases holding a key card.

They told her they had been assigned the room by reception.

"I asked them if they'd come into this room and they said, 'yeah, we're really sorry, we've just checked in and this is where we've been allocated'," she said.

"I said to them, 'well, no, I've actually been here since last night and I'm here until tomorrow.'

"They were extremely apologetic and, as I say, mortified - I felt incredibly vulnerable, you know, in a state of undress."

'You've paid for that space to have privacy and safety'

Jade spoke to reception staff as she left the hotel to go to the wedding.

"You're not expecting anybody to be able to get into the room, that you've paid for to have privacy and safety. That's what a hotel is there for and that was entirely invaded.

"Initially I was angry but I knew I had to leave for the wedding in about 10 minutes time and I thought, right, I just need to get dressed.

"So I went to speak to reception when I was on my way out. This is when I started to feel a bit more anxious about it and a bit more worried about it.

"The staff were aware because the couple had gone down to reception after they'd tried to come into the room. They said, 'We're really sorry that's happened. We did come up to speak to you, but there was a do not disturb sign on the door," she said.

Jade said she still enjoyed her friend's special day but grew more anxious as time went on.

"I told the staff it really wasn't OK and it is really inappropriate for that to have been allowed to happen. If I wasn't going to a wedding, I'd be grabbing all my stuff and I'd be leaving immediately.

"But I needed to leave to go to the wedding, unfortunately. I still had a good day, but it did colour the event.

"I didn't feel safe, I didn't feel comfortable, and I would rather go and get my things and get a train back to Edinburgh."

Jade is concerned her experience shows not enough has been done regarding safety issues at the hotel chain.

Earlier this year, a man was jailed for sexually assaulting a woman in a Travelodge hotel room in Maidenhead, Berkshire, after he lied to get a key to her room.

A subsequent independent report found the woman was fundamentally failed by Travelodge, which apologised "unreservedly" and made "immediate changes" to its door key policy.

Jade said: "Incidents in the past that took place in Travelodge hotels are horrendous and the hotel chain is portraying a narrative that they have updated all their systems and security measures and procedures and things.

"When actually my experience is showing that incidents like this are still happening and people's privacy, their security and their safety is still potentially being put at risk, which isn't OK.

"I have no desire to stay in a Travelodge ever again, and I think staying in any hotel as a solo female guest will give me some level of anxiety in the future."

Couple woke to find shirtless intruder in Travelodge room

A Travelodge spokesperson said it had immediately conducted a full investigation into the incident to understand what went wrong.

And they said the company had now taken steps to prevent this from happening in the future.

"We are very sorry for this customer's experience. Safety and security is our priority and any case of an unauthorised person entering a guest's room is a significant cause for concern, and should not happen," a statement said.

"We immediately contacted this guest to apologise and carried out a comprehensive investigation, taking swift internal action.

"We continue to take rigorous steps to reinforce safety for all our guests."

articles.title: Landeed, Fractal Analytics: The AI start-ups fixing India's broken roads and messy land records
articles.summary: From legal-tech to healthcare, dozens of Indian AI start-ups are solving uniquely Indian challenges.
articles.body:
In 2020, Sanjay Mandava flew down from Chicago to Chennai in southern India to resolve a personal land dispute.

Over the next few months, he was running around between government offices to access a dozen records that would conclusively prove that the property belonged to his family.

Just a sale deed dating back to when his parents bought the land was not enough. Authorities asked him to produce a string of other documents.

Frustrated by the experience, he built Landeed - an AI-led digital platform that enables users to aggregate fragmented, multi-source land-records, verify titles and conduct legal checks at the click of a few buttons , across 24 states in India.

He's solving a problem that is uniquely Indian.

"In the US or UK, when you purchase a property, the government verifies ownership. In India by contrast, we follow presumptive titling - the buyer is responsible for establishing ownership. A sale deed merely records the transaction - multiple other documents may be needed to prove title," Mandava told the BBC.

These include building certificates, property tax receipts and land survey maps among others.

The system is rife for misuse - property disputes account for a bulk of civil litigation cases in the country where some 80% of household wealth is held in real estate.

Landeed has mapped large swathes of India using geo-spatial technology and data from state land revenue departments, registration offices, survey records and municipal databases.

Using this, it has linked registered properties to their official land identification and survey numbers and ownership records.

An additional AI-layer can read these titles, extract information and spot inconsistencies within minutes - a process that takes lawyers and brokers several days.

With the largest repository of title data in the country, consisting of 1.8 billion documents, the app is now used by millions of individual and enterprise customers while doing real estate transactions.

The app is among a burgeoning list of Indian start-ups trying to address some of India's most complex challenges in sectors ranging from legal-tech to healthcare, infrastructure, education and agriculture using AI.

Unlike the US and China which have a global dominance in building frontier language models like ChatGPT, India's AI revolution is happening downstream in data centre infrastructure and consumer applications rather than in research.

Start-ups are solving issues for everything from pothole detection to tribal language translation to assisting overworked public-health professionals with medical tasks - often working with highly fragmented, multilingual datasets in extremely cost sensitive industries.

Bengaluru-based YouTube teacher Gaurav Sen's AI app detects potholes using a dash-cam, satellite-based navigation and an AI vision model to analyse images.

It then identifies civic officials responsible for fixing them and sends them this data. He got viral attention recently given how widespread the menace of potholes is across India's urban sprawls.

On last count, there are at least half a dozen other similar offerings that map and report road damage to authorities across the country.

"A municipal corporation can take the app and use it on public buses and taxis, to access real-time, updated data on road conditions," Sen told the BBC.

In Mumbai on India's western coast, Fractal Analytics - among the few Indian listed AI companies - has deployed its AI tool "Vaidya" in hospitals run by the local civic authority.

The app allows citizens to receive AI-generated, simplified summaries of their lab reports in multiple languages, identify nearby healthcare facilities based on their needs and gives doctors AI-guided pre-consultation support such as medical history and medication details of patients.

It also provides hospital administrators with a public health dashboard based on aggregated, anonymous insights from lab reports accessed through its tie-up with municipal hospitals, giving them crucial visibility into emerging infections or other disease trends.

This boom has led to a surge in funding for AI start-ups - up 265% year-on-year according to Inc42 , a start-up information platform. They raised over $1bn in the first nine months of this year amid a relatively muted fundraising environment for the broader ecosystem.

Yet, these companies face an uphill task in commercialising their ideas and taking them beyond pilot.

"The cost of building in India is sometimes much higher than what Indian customers are willing to pay," Fractal's co-founder Srikanth Velamakanni told the BBC at his sprawling office overlooking Mumbai's film city.

"The computing power needed to run an AI model is the same whether it is built in India or the US - but American customers have a far bigger paying capacity than those here."

Indian AI founders are also being forced to build around scarcity, with availability of high quality chips at the right scale and price, a major impediment for many.

"I believe I am building one of the most impactful things for this country," says Mandava.

"But I am starved for GPUs [chips that perform millions of calculations and help train AI models]. I have a hellish time trying to acquire them," he says.

The country has promised its start-ups 38,000 GPUs through its government-led AI mission , but demand for this compute power is far greater than supply.

Cumbersome regulation and bureaucracy are other major challenges.

Without these fundamental issues being addressed, there's a risk that Indian AI companies will build shallow solutions that a next generation of founders will immediately make redundant, say experts.

"Someone like a Google will probably laugh if I tell them of my pilot. To make it sustainable and hard to replicate, it will have to be much more sophisticated," says Sen, displaying a self-awareness of where his product currently stands.

From a lack of experienced talent to the struggle to turn successful pilots into recurring government contracts to heavy dependence on expensive foreign technology, Indian founders are powering through many odds.

"We can still do it. We don't want protection, but propel us, give us the weapons to compete against the best," Mandava says, when asked what he wants from policymakers.

"To quote Jay-Z - I can't help the poor if I'm one of them," he adds.

articles.title: We were priced out of the market, so we bought a home with strangers
articles.summary: People who can't afford to get on the housing ladder are buying homes with people they don't know.
articles.body:
When Elizabeth and Tom Wilcox realised they could never afford to buy the home they wanted for themselves and their two children, they decided to take a leap of faith.

They'd find another couple with young kids, complete strangers to them, and propose that they go halves on a property and all move in together.

Based in Vancouver, which has long had some of the highest house prices in Canada, the Wilcoxes were desperate to buy a home that had a back garden for their children to play in.

"We wanted a house with a yard that could fit a trampoline, in a walkable neighbourhood, but we couldn't afford it," says Elizabeth, a project manager in the healthcare sector.

With a budget of C$1m ($700,000; £500,000) all they could hope for was a small apartment with a balcony at best.

That was when Elizabeth came up with the idea of buying with another family.

They placed an advert in a local estate agent's e-newsletter, but it took two years before they finally met a family whom they clicked with – Ashley Pullman and her husband and two children.

In 2023, the Wilcoxes and the Pullmans co-bought a six-bedroom, detached house, complete with a back garden, for C$1.85m.

The two families split the deposit of C$250,000, and continue to go halves on the monthly mortgage payments of C$3,900. They also divide bills and other expenses equally, such as any necessary home repairs.

Elizabeth says the arrangement has saved both families "tens of thousands of dollars".

While there is no official data available for the number of people buying homes with people they previously didn't know, Parimal Gosal says he has seen a big increase in interest in Toronto as a response to high property prices.

Gosal is the founder and CEO of Husmates, an app and website that connects people in Canada's largest city who are looking to potentially buy a home with a stranger.

It can be seen as "a financial relationship, and that takes emotions out of it", he says.

It's unclear how common this phenomenon is elsewhere in the world. David Hollingworth, from British mortgage broker L&C, says while he hasn't come across it himself, he thinks it also happens in the UK, though is "very niche".

"I remember that before Covid-19 there was a matchmaking event in a London pub, like speed dating, for people looking to buy a house with a stranger," he says. "How successful this was I don' t know."

Three years on, the Wilcoxes and the Pullmans say their living arrangement is still working out.

While each family has some private living spaces, such as their own kitchens, they share the big basement-level living room, which includes a home gym in one corner, and a shared freezer.

"If someone says they're in the basement to work out, we know not to go there for a bit, and it's never been an issue," says Elizabeth.

Ashley agrees that there are no problems. "Maybe it's arrogance but my husband and I felt like we were the type of people who could live with strangers," she says.

Sabrina Bowman, a freelance business consultant in Toronto, has co-owned a home with two other housemates since 2018. When she signed on the dotted line and moved in she didn't know one of the other two people.

While Sabrina says she isn't comfortable sharing the exact financial details, she says they decided to divide up the deposit and mortgage payments based on each of their levels of income.

She says any household disputes can be addressed early with open discussions. "What is important to us is having structures to communicate about everything that happens in the home."

They have regular house meetings where they discuss chores, financial issues, birthday celebrations, and any disagreements.

"It's great to see people be honest about something they may not be comfortable about and for us to find a solution to that problem," Sabrina says.

In the case of both Sabrina's house in Toronto and the Wilcox and Pullman property in Vancouver, they have legal agreements in place in case someone wants to sell up and move out.

For both homes, reasonable notice periods are specified, and for Sabrina's, the departing housemate is required to give those remaining the first opportunity to buy their share.

Toronto real estate lawyer Tanya Walker says such legal assurances are vital. "You need something legally binding instead of a bunch of emails and Facebook messages that can be too messy to collect if a dispute comes up," Walker says.

Back in Vancouver, Elizabeth says that neither family has a timeframe for how long they will live in the house. "All of us are really happy with the set-up and location so it would be hard to move.

"I can't put a price on how it felt to watch the kids jump on the trampoline for the first time, or run in circles on our patch of green grass."

articles.title: The young people caught up in Britain's Neets crisis
articles.summary: BBC News speaks to four of the million young people aged 16 to 24 who are not in work, education or training.
articles.body:
The number of young people who are not in work, at school or in college is both an economic and moral crisis, a landmark report into the problem will say later.

The 241-page report, by ex-Labour minister Alan Milburn, will set out a raft of recommendations for the government to consider.

Ahead of its publication, four young people who are not in education, employment or training - those dubbed as "Neets" - tell us why they can't get a job and how the government could help them get one.

Michael: 'Everything is experience, experience, experience'

Michael, 19, who lives with his dad in the Wirral, says he dropped out of college and spent a year at home after his social anxiety "got really bad". It is "very easy" to fall out of the system, he says, if there is little support available.

Michael's story is not unique. There has been a large rise in anxiety and mental health problems in young people .

About one in five Neets have a mental health condition, according to 2025 data from the Department for Education (DfE) - more than double the rate in 2012.

Having signed up for Universal Credit, Michael was put in touch with the Merseyside Youth Association to help him find a job. He says mentors there have helped him improve his mental health, which led to him dropping out of college during his A-levels. He says that left him trapped inside his bedroom.

He says jobs in his area are scarce and those that do come up tend to go to older people with more experience. Michael says he is trapped in the cycle of not having the experience needed to build more.

"Everything is experience, experience, experience - that's the one thing that I always used to hear when going for jobs on my own without the help," he says.

We followed Michael for a day, meeting him after his 05:00 start for a work experience shift at a local supermarket that the Merseyside Youth Association helped him get.

Lots of Neets receive Universal Credit. For under-25s, the standard rate is £338.58 a month , which Michael gets. For some people who cannot work because of a health condition, disability or long-term illness, an additional £217.26 to £429.80 per month may be available.

Ahead of the publication of his full review, it was reported that Milburn would recommend young people should no longer be able to claim those additional health-related benefits, as part of a major overhaul of the welfare system .

Michael acknowledges some young people may be "taking advantage" of the benefits system, but says most "just want the money to get by so they can get a job".

More recently, he has been doing shifts at the Merseyside Youth Centre's on-site cafe to gain more much-needed experience. His hope is to be in a steady job earning money this time next year, with space to have his own art studio one day.

"From three months ago I'm a different person," he says. "I can do stuff, keep going."

Maariyah: 'I send 20 job applications a week'

Maariyah, a 22-year-old history and politics graduate, finished her university course last summer. Her dream is to work in museums.

However, she is currently unemployed and looking for any paid job after working a temporary six-month contract for a housing association earlier this year.

She says she spends hours each day in her local library - where she feels more able to focus than she can at home - submitting at least 20 tailored job applications a week.

Those who have not achieved GCSE-level qualifications are more likely to remain Neet for longer periods - however, an estimated one in 10 Neets are university graduates .

Maariyah says she is applying for roles in retail and restaurants, alongside unpaid work experience opportunities in the heritage sector.

But she says she has also been rejected for voluntary roles because they had too many applicants, or because she does not have enough experience. "I'm actively going out of my way to do unpaid work, only to get rejected from these positions," she says.

Not hearing back from employers "happens so often now that's it's like second nature", she says, adding that she finds it frustrating that many of her applications are likely to be screened by AI before a real person sees them.

On the day we meet, Maariyah heads to the job centre for her Universal Credit appointment after a library job application session. She says she has noticed an improvement in the support she gets there since she first received the benefit in 2025.

This time, she will be getting some mandatory hospitality training, which she says she is "really glad" to have.

She feels there is a growing sense of disillusionment among others her age. Being on benefits has become normalised because it is so hard to find a job, she adds.

It makes her feel that going to a good university, getting certain grades and doing extracurricular activities "doesn't make a difference in the end".

"I would like employers to give young people a chance to gain experience and take a chance on hard-working people who at the end of the day want a job so that they can contribute to our economy and contribute to their own lives."

Matthieu: 'You might be surprised what people can do'

Matthieu, 19, from Edgware in north-west London, is autistic and currently volunteers at a gardening club and a computer repair shop.

We meet him in Finsbury Park, where he is helping to mulch some newly planted trees. Working in nature is calming, he says.

He is looking for work with the support of the charity Ambitious About Autism and his mentor, Annie. He previously did a year-long supported internship with the Whittington hospital.

Matthieu says speaking to people face-to-face there helped his confidence and he enjoyed being part of the team. At his family home, Matthieu's mentor Annie tells us that not having maths and English GCSE qualifications is a barrier to finding employment.

Matthieu says he's more of a manual worker and wants to work in a factory, warehouse or doing deliveries, so that he can contribute financially for his family.

Those with learning difficulties, including autism, make up an estimated 12% of Neets, DfE data shows. Milburn's interim report , which was published in the summer, said 45% of Neets reported having a disability. He said the situation for young disabled people was "devastating".

To make work accessible to him, Matthieu says he would need an employer to take their time with him. He says: "I don't learn that quickly." But he thinks it would be worth it.

"Honestly, you might be surprised what the people can do when you take the time with them and give them that chance," Matthieu says.

Many employers say they can not afford to do so following rises to National Insurance contributions and the minimum wage , which is increasing further as part of announcements made in October's Budget.

Some businesses have told the BBC they are struggling to provide new jobs for young people due to these changes, as well as other factors like rising energy bills.

Although finding work is hard, Matthieu says he remains hopeful because of the support from his internship and job coach.

Alex, 20, from St Helens, has been looking for work for a year. She struggles with anxiety and is looking for roles as a cleaner or in retail. She also shares caring responsibilities for her mum with her other family members.

We meet her at Spear, an employment and mindset coaching programme. Alex says her dream is to work with animals. She says she had been studying Level 3 animal management at college before dropping out last year because of her mental health.

"I was so burnt out," she says. "I was struggling to get out of bed, I couldn't do anything. I was dragging myself to college. I was like, 'No, I need to have a break for a bit and try and figure out what to do after that'."

Building up her resilience is something she now works on with a mentor, as well as job applications.

Alex says she is applying for "anything and everything" and wants to get off benefits. She is also currently receiving Universal Credit, which she says is "all the money that I've got until I get a job and I'm earning more".

When asked what she thinks about potential benefits cuts for young people out of work, Alex says not being able to access benefits would "make life so much worse".

And she says trying to find work in a place like St Helens is harder, because many businesses in the town centre have either "gone or moved or shut down".

"Lots of people think, 'well, young people just don't want to work,'" she says. "But we do. We so desperately want to work. Places don't want to hire us."

Milburn has already said the system isn't working for everyone, and that serious action is needed to avoid young Neets becoming a "lost generation".

articles.title: Illegal alien accused of attempted murder at large after Rikers release despite ICE detainer: DHS
articles.summary: Delon Raymond Jaundoo, a Guyanese citizen in the United States illegally, was freed from Rikers Island despite an ICE detainer, according to DHS.
articles.body: A Guyanese citizen living in the United States illegally remains at large after being released from custody in New York City earlier this month, despite facing multiple violent felony charges and an active federal immigration detainer, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). DHS officials stated that Delon Raymond Jaundoo was arrested in Brooklyn on charges including attempted murder, first- and second-degree assault, criminal use of a firearm, and multiple counts of criminal possession of a loaded weapon. His prior criminal record also includes an arrest for third-degree assault. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) lodged an immigration detainer for Jaundoo on April 29, which the New York City Department of Correction declined to honor, allowing him to be released from Rikers Island. MANHUNT UNDERWAY FOR VIOLENT ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT WHO WAS RELEASED UNDER NYC SANCTUARY POLICIES Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin criticized New York’s sanctuary policies following the release, arguing that state and local laws prevent cooperation with federal immigration authorities even in cases involving violent offenses. Jaundoo lawfully entered the country during the Obama administration but overstayed his authorized stay, which expired in January 2015, according to DHS. "Despite these violent charges, sanctuary politicians in New York refused to honor ICE’s detainer and released this criminal back onto the streets to put more American lives in danger," Mullin said in a statement. "Under Governor Kathy Hochul, New York has become a hotbed of illegal alien crime." DHS SECRETARY BASHES NEW YORK LEADERSHIP AFTER ANNOUNCING THOUSANDS OF ARRESTS IN SWEEPING OPERATION "The sooner we put an end to these reckless sanctuary policies, the sooner we can all work together to make America safe again," he added. Kathy Hochul took effect in August barring local authorities from cooperating with federal immigration officials. DHS stated that several other illegal immigrants arrested for or convicted of violent crimes, including murder, arson, assault, and rape, have similarly been released from custody under the state's current policies.
