articles.title: Ethiopia Moyale clashes disrupt livelihoods as territorial dispute deepens
articles.summary: The country’s unresolved Oromia-Somali border dispute fuels renewed violence, displacing thousands.
articles.body:
Moyale, Ethiopia – Fighting involving police and armed groups affiliated with Ethiopia’s Oromia and Somali regional administrations has disrupted daily life and trade in the southern Borana Zone, as efforts to resolve a longstanding territorial dispute have yet to produce a lasting settlement.

The violence, which escalated in the border town of Moyale in October, has spread to surrounding areas, including the neighbouring districts of Arero and Wachile, leaving communities insecure and uncertain when normal life will resume.

The disruption has affected livelihoods across several parts of the zone, particularly the livestock trade – a major source of income for rural communities. Residents have reported interruptions to business activities and transport services.

A resident of Moyale town, who asked not to be named for security reasons, told Al Jazeera that people remained fearful as tensions persisted between forces affiliated with the two regional administrations.

The resident said gunfire, especially at night, had heightened personal safety concerns, while violence had restricted movement around the town and made routine activities increasingly difficult. Businesses, people raising livestock and transport operators had also been affected, leaving residents uncertain about when the situation would return to normal.

A territorial dispute reignites violence

According to Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED), the latest escalation began on October 18, when Somali regional police clashed with ethnic Oromo militia members following the opening of a Somali regional administration office and the raising of its flag in a disputed locality of Moyale.

The conflict monitor’s East Africa senior analyst, Jalale Getachew Birru, reported that a 13-year-old Oromo girl was killed during the confrontation. However, accounts of how she died differ: some people said she was caught in crossfire, while others claimed she was killed after trying to remove the flag.

Members of the Ethiopian National Defence Force intervened and stopped the initial fighting, according to ACLED. The following day, Oromo residents staged a demonstration against the office opening and the girl’s death, blocking the main road and forcing businesses to close.

Elders and security officials from both sides later agreed to remove the Somali regional flag and suspend the office’s opening. However, the agreement did not prevent further confrontations. ACLED reported that Somali residents also demonstrated against the arrangement on October 20, closing the main road and disrupting transport services.

Fighting escalated again on October 22, when Somali regional police clashed with Oromia regional police and Oromo militia members in several locations in Moyale. ACLED also reported clashes involving Oromo and Somali militias in parts of Arero and Wachile districts.

The violence is rooted in longstanding disagreements over administrative boundaries, political representation and access to land and natural resources. These disputes have repeatedly fuelled tensions between Borana Oromo and Somali communities along the regional border.

Federal government under pressure to intervene

A security official familiar with the situation in Moyale told Al Jazeera that clashes were continuing and that attempts to broker an agreement between representatives of the Oromia and Somali regional administrations had failed. He said resolving the crisis required direct and immediate involvement by the federal government.

The federal government’s role has consequently become a central question in efforts to contain the violence. Although members of the Ethiopian National Defence Force intervened during the initial October 18 confrontation, ACLED documented further clashes involving regional police and militia members from October 22 onwards.

The crisis has also drawn attention beyond Ethiopia’s borders. On November 9, Kenya’s Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi said he had spoken with his Ethiopian counterpart and urged the government in Addis Ababa to help restore stability so that people who had fled into Kenya could return home.

Reporting by Kenya’s The Star newspaper said Mudavadi put the number of Ethiopians who had crossed into Kenya at approximately 40,000 at the time. He said the Ethiopian government had assured Kenya that it would work towards restoring normality.

Unresolved boundaries and political tensions

Cameron Hudson, a political and security analyst and former director for African affairs at the US National Security Council, said the crisis reflected wider challenges facing Ethiopia’s federal system and its management of regional disputes.

Hudson said federal forces were already preoccupied with security challenges elsewhere in the country. He also pointed to a perception among Somali communities that Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and his Prosperity Party favour the Oromo, Abiy’s ethnic group.

Hudson said previous mediation efforts had largely failed because the territorial dispute along the regional border remained unresolved.

The historical background includes a referendum organised on October 24, 2004, to determine the administration of 463 small communities along the Oromia-Somali regional border, according to Ethiopia’s National Election Board.

However, research by Boku Tache, published in a doctoral thesis at the Norwegian University of Life Sciences in 2008, found that the referendum was conducted in Liban and parts of Arero, while the Moyale case remained unresolved.

The research also examined how displacement, competing claims over grazing land and access to traditional resources contributed to tensions between Borana and Somali communities. These historical disputes continue to provide important context for the current confrontation.

Hudson added that successive Ethiopian governments had failed to engage local communities to address the underlying causes of territorial tensions, instead responding after violence had erupted.

The humanitarian consequences have extended beyond Ethiopia. On October 28, the United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR) said local authorities estimated that up to 50,000 people had crossed into Kenya since October 22 to escape the fighting. The agency said registration and verification were continuing, meaning the figure remained provisional.

Many of those arriving in Kenya were women and children, according to the UNHCR, which identified food, drinking water, emergency shelter, sanitation and healthcare as urgent needs.

For residents in the affected areas, immediate priorities remain the restoration of security and the resumption of livelihoods. With the territorial dispute unresolved and the two regional administrations yet to reach a lasting agreement, uncertainty continues over when affected communities will be able to return to normal life.

“The federal government is ultimately responsible for addressing violence, even along regional borders,” Hudson told Al Jazeera.

articles.title: UK seeks closer ties with EU after Brexit fail
articles.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham says UK lost more than it gained after its divorce from the bloc.
articles.body:
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the Brexit promise failed to deliver for the United Kingdom and that the country needs to reset its relationship with the European Union to combat growing global isolationism.

During a speech at the Lord Mayor’s Banquet in London on Monday, Burnham compared the outcome of Britain’s divorce from the EU, triggered by a 2016 referendum, to the Hans Christian Andersen fairy tale “The Emperor’s New Clothes”, in which no one is willing to tell the ruler that he is, in fact, naked.

“I do try to say things as I see them,” Burnham said. “And to be frank, we have lost more than we have gained in the last 10 years. The hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain.”

The remarks come ahead of a UK-EU summit in Brussels on Friday, which Burnham said could deliver “real improvements in people’s everyday lives in areas of the country that have felt neglected for too long”.

Any deal, he said, would have to pass three tests: it would have to be consistent with Labour’s manifesto and red lines, improve the Brexit deal to align with what people voted for in 2016 and pass his Makerfield Test, his benchmark for ensuring real improvements for people in parts of the UK that have long felt neglected.

The meeting is a key step in his pledge to reset relations with the 27-nation bloc a decade after the UK voted to leave and six years after its 2020 departure.

The UK is expected to seal a deal on trading food and drink, and make agreements on energy and emissions and a plan to let young people work for limited periods across Britain and the EU.

Burnham said the promise of the pro-Brexit campaign that Britain would “take back control” of its borders, laws and economy had not been delivered. Trade with EU countries has dropped sharply, and estimates of the economic damage range from 4 percent to 8 percent of the UK’s gross domestic product, he said.

Seeking to draw a line under a decade of political turmoil that has made him Britain’s seventh prime minister since 2016, Burnham said the UK was back on the world stage. He argued the country is well positioned to lead in an era of renewed international cooperation because of its experience since 2016.

“Brexit was the first domino to fall in a global move towards more isolationism and protectionism,” he said. “It is exactly what our enemies wanted. Russia wanted disunity within NATO and a weaker Europe.”

Burnham said that he will open a discussion with EU partners on Britain’s long-term relationship with the bloc soon after the Brussels summit. His spokesperson Tom Wells said on Monday that “no assumptions are being made” and “the British public will be the boss of any outcome”.

Until the next national election, Burnham remains bound by the pledge of Keir Starmer, whom he replaced as centre-left Labour Party leader and prime minister, not to rejoin the bloc’s tariff-free customs union or frictionless single market for goods, services and workers.

Erasing that pledge would reignite a subject that split the country: the 2016 referendum vote was 52 percent in favour of leaving the EU and 48 percent in support of remaining.

articles.title: Ukraine holds peace talks with US, Europe as conflict escalates
articles.summary: Kushner reports progress towards a deal, but Moscow says it has not agreed to European participation in the next talks.
articles.body:
Ukraine has held new talks with United States and European officials on ending the war with Russia, hours before Kyiv’s mayor reported strikes on two bridges in the capital.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described Monday’s online discussions with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and European representatives as “not easy”. But he said participants had agreed to meet in Berlin with the “Coalition of the Willing”, a group of countries supporting Ukraine, as the US and Europe step up peace talks this week.

“Diplomatic processes are actively underway and we hope that these efforts will not be in vain,” Zelenskyy said in his nightly address.

He also warned that Ukrainian intelligence indicated Russia was preparing major strikes that night and throughout Tuesday.

Later on Monday, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said preliminary reports indicated that the North and South bridges across the Dnipro River had been hit. Air defence units were operating, and Reuters news agency witnesses heard a series of loud explosions.

Ukraine on Monday struck a key bridge and targeted oil refineries in what Russian defence ministry data indicated was the biggest overnight drone attack on Russia since the start of full-scale war in 2022. The Crimea Bridge was again struck overnight, with nearly 200 drones intercepted near Moscow, according to Telegram statements.

US envoy reports progress, warns of difficult choices

Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, said Washington was making progress towards an agreement in coordination with Russia, Ukraine and Europe.

“Important challenges remain, and a final agreement will require difficult decisions,” he wrote on X.

He said he and Witkoff had also spoken with Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov about the next steps. Their discussions included how to arrange direct engagement between Europe and Russia so each could hear the other’s concerns and proposals.

The exchanges followed last week’s talks in Abu Dhabi , where US, Ukrainian and Russian officials met together for the first time in nine months. Those negotiations produced an agreement on a prisoner exchange but no breakthrough on ending the war.

Witkoff and Kushner later met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow and said European representatives would join the next round. On Monday, Moscow disputed that assertion.

Europe prepares to join, Moscow withholds agreement

Zelenskyy said representatives from France, Germany, Britain, Italy and Poland had participated fully in Monday’s discussion and would have the same representation in future meetings with Russian negotiators.

Ushakov said Russia had not agreed to expand the talks beyond the existing Russian, Ukrainian and US delegations. No date had been agreed for the next round, he added.

European governments, meanwhile, were preparing their negotiating team while maintaining pressure on Moscow.

Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee welcomed renewed talks and the agreement on EU representation following diplomatic meetings in Abu Dhabi and Dublin last week. But she said, “Russia has clearly not changed its position.”

Speaking ahead of Monday’s meeting of EU foreign ministers in Brussels, McEntee said 113 new sanctions on Russia were intended to maintain pressure on Moscow “as it intensified attacks on civilians and critical infrastructure during the winter”.

“We are also working to ensure Ukraine has the finance and the military support it needs while advancing Ukraine’s path to EU membership,” she said.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Russia wanted a lasting peace rather than a temporary ceasefire that would allow Ukraine to recover from the damage inflicted by Russian forces.

He said Moscow sought peace lasting “years, even centuries”, adding that negotiations were complex and could take considerable time.

Separately, Trump said he would discuss the war with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Putin in China, saying he believed Putin wanted to end the war.

“I think he’s backing down a little bit,” Trump told reporters. “Frankly, I think he’d like to see it finish.”

The planned Berlin meeting would allow Ukraine and its supporters to agree on their next negotiating steps. Russia had yet to accept their proposed representation in the talks that would follow.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, right, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy [File: Ralf Hirschberger/Pool via AP Photo]

articles.title: Hillary Clinton picks a foreign politician she believes is now the ‘leader of the free world’
articles.summary: Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton argued Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney may be the current "leader of the free world" instead of President Donald Trump.
articles.body: Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton argued during an interview aired Sunday that if any politician qualifies as the current "leader of the free world," it would be Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney. MS NOW host Rachel Maddow interviewed Clinton at the Temple Emanu-El Streicker Center in New York City and asked, "Do you think that there is a leader of the free world right now?" "Maybe Mark Carney," Clinton said. "That’s what I was going to ask," Maddow said. "He’s certainly articulating a vision of the free countries of the world and of — of the liberty-loving nations of the world that is about being stronger together." CARNEY CASTS HIMSELF AS NATO DEFENDER AMID TRUMP BEEF, DESPITE CANADA MISSING KEY BENCHMARK FOR DECADES The relationship between the United States and Canada has been strained following President Donald Trump's suggestions that Canada become the 51st U.S. state and his decision to impose tariffs on Canadian goods. Clinton also argued that while some individual European leaders stood out, the continent as a whole was too disorganized. "And, you know, there are some good individual European leaders, but Europe has got to get itself organized so that, you know, the sum of the parts adds up to some kind of a whole and be able to do a better job at making some tough decisions, particularly with respect to Ukraine," she said. "They need to release the $250 million of Russian assets that are frozen in those Belgian banks and use it to defend Ukraine, just for starters." "So if they can begin to make some collective decisions, then I think you’ll see other leaders emerge," Clinton continued. "But there’s going to be, as you know, Rachel, some very consequential elections in Europe this year, like the presidency of France. And if a populist pro-Putin party emerges with a leader who is very close to Putin and very beholden to Putin, Marine Le Pen, becomes the president of France, then we have new problems that we’re going to have to deal with." TRUMP’S PROPOSED RUSSIA DEAL RAISES NATO ALARM AS EX-COMMANDER WARNS PUTIN SEEKS INFLUENCE OVER EUROPE Earlier in the interview, Clinton argued that Trump had done "immeasurable damage" to America’s standing on the world stage with foreign policy that she described as "dangerous and incoherent.’ She also accused Trump of catering to "strongmen leaders." "We are, unfortunately, seeing someone who admires strongmen leaders, thinks he is one, and believes in the old-fashioned concept of spheres of power," Clinton said. "And honestly, I don’t think it’s exaggerating to say that he’s perfectly fine with Putin doing whatever he wants with Ukraine and the rest of Europe." "He’s perfectly fine with Xi doing whatever he wants with Asia, as long as he can dominate the Western Hemisphere, and that all of them are some kind of triumvirate that is going to decide what the rest of us are capable of doing and what kind of society we will live under," she added. White House spokesman Davis Ingle told Fox News Digital, "President Trump is creating good-paying jobs, securing trillions of dollars in investments, and positioning our country to dominate the remainder of the 21st century. Meanwhile, Crooked Hillary Clinton is still whining about her spectacular 2016 election defeat. It’s time for Hillary to move on." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Morgan Murphy, a former White House official and former Pentagon press secretary, told Fox News Digital in response to Clinton's comments, "Canada's economy is chasing Mississippi's, and its armed forces couldn't scare the Salvation Army. It’s obvious Hillary still can’t admit the obvious: she lost [to] Trump, and he’s still the leader of the free world." Theo Wold, a former White House deputy assistant for domestic policy under Trump, also criticized Clinton's comments. "Canada’s PM Carney is nothing close to being the leader of the free world," Wold told Fox News Digital. "The Canadian economy is contracting; Canadian culture is at its weakest point as a consequence of mass immigration and proliferating crime and budget problems; separatist movements across the Canadian federation are gaining strength; and most of all, to the extent Canada projects power at all, it does so only from within the sphere of U.S. power projection and military might in the Western Hemisphere, making Canada at best a younger sibling piggybacking on America’s power projection around the world." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Carney, pretending to be 2026’s Marshall Tito, used several high-profile speeches to criticize the America First movement and pitch a small state ‘non-aligned movement,’" he added. "There are no takers for this idiotic gambit outside of EU cultural elites in the dying capitals of Europe."

articles.title: Irish court jails man for life over Dublin knife attack that sparked riots
articles.summary: Three children and a woman were injured in the attack outside a central Dublin school in 2023.
articles.body:
A 52-year-old man has been sentenced to life behind bars for the attempted murder of three children in Dublin on November 23, 2023, in an attack that triggered rioting and looting in the Irish capital.

Riad Bouchaker, an Algerian national and Irish citizen, was sentenced at the Central Criminal Court in Dublin on Monday after being found guilty in July on eight charges arising from the knife attack outside a school nearly three years ago.

His victims included a five-year-old girl, a six-year-old girl, a five-year-old boy and a woman in her mid-30s.

The youngest girl was stabbed in the heart, resulting in severe disability after her brain was deprived of oxygen for 40 minutes following the attack.

The girl, who is now eight, cannot speak and communicates only by blinking. She uses a wheelchair and is fed through a tube in her stomach because she is unable to swallow safely.

Bouchaker was also found guilty of assaulting childcare worker Leanne Flynn, who suffered serious injuries as she tried to protect the children.

Speaking outside the court, Garda Superintendent Colm Murphy, the senior investigating officer, acknowledged the actions of those who intervened, the Press Association reported.

“I just want to take this opportunity to acknowledge the actions of those that immediately reacted to the situation as it unfolded, in particular to Leanne Flynn, who undoubtedly her actions on the day saved lives,” he said.

Within hours of the attack, false information about the suspect’s identity spread online, fuelling anger among anti-immigration activists and far-right groups.

The worst rioting seen in the Irish capital for decades erupted in the city centre as crowds clashed with police, set vehicles on fire and looted shops.

The violence shocked the country and triggered days of debate over immigration, online misinformation and public order.

Nearly 100 people were arrested, and more than 80 were charged with offences.

Bouchaker had pleaded not guilty to three counts of attempted murder and three counts of assault causing harm.

He also denied one count each of intentionally or recklessly causing serious harm and brandishing a dangerous weapon, a kitchen knife.

Judge Tony Hunt told the jury that two years before the attack, Bouchaker had suffered from a benign brain tumour that required surgery.

Hunt also said that due to interventions by bystanders immediately after the attack, Bouchaker suffered a head injury that required hospital treatment.

He was found fit to stand trial, and “there is no suggestion that he was suffering mental disorder at the time of the incident”, the judge said.

Evidence was heard from more than 80 witnesses, including eyewitnesses, emergency responders, police and forensic experts.

articles.title: Yemeni army reports 661 attacks on Houthis as group advances towards Aden
articles.summary: Yemen’s army reports 173 Houthi fighters killed or wounded as government forces reposition to defend Aden.
articles.body:
Yemen’s army has said it carried out 661 attacks against Houthi positions across several fronts, killing or wounding 173 fighters, as government forces continue their military campaign amid Houthi territorial gains in the country’s southwest.

Military spokesperson Colonel Majed al-Nuzaili said on Monday that the operations, conducted as part of the ongoing “Dawn of Yemen” offensive, included 15 air strikes, 526 artillery attacks, 53 drone strikes and 67 rocket attacks.

In a statement on X, al-Nuzaili said the attacks had destroyed or damaged 71 military vehicles and pieces of equipment, as well as command-and-control centres, observation posts and fortifications.

He said government forces, backed by the Popular Resistance, were continuing to confront Houthi movements in the provinces of Taiz, Marib and al-Jawf, while operations were also under way on southern fronts.

The military said it would continue its offensive until it achieved its objectives, while taking precautions to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure.

The latest operations followed a series of battlefield setbacks for government-aligned forces, which have withdrawn from strategic positions near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and are repositioning to defend Aden, the temporary capital of Yemen’s internationally recognised government.

Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry reported that the Houthis had cut off a key government supply route along the Red Sea coast, forcing troops to abandon several positions as concerns grew over a possible Houthi offensive towards Aden.

The military escalation coincided with a political development, as Yemen’s parliament unanimously approved a bill designating the Houthis a “terrorist organisation” and criminalising their activities, financing and supply of weapons.

According to the state-run Saba news agency, the bill provides for prosecuting those involved in violations attributed to the group, freezing and confiscating affiliated assets, and imposing tougher penalties for offences, including attacks on civilians, planting landmines and targeting international shipping.

The legislation will now be submitted to Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, for enactment.

The latest developments come six weeks after government forces launched “Dawn of Yemen” on October 5, seeking to regain territory controlled by the Houthis, including the capital, Sanaa.

articles.title: The bar-headed goose that flies over the Himalayas: How it survives one of the world's most extraordinary bird migrations
articles.summary: Imagine flying over the Himalayas, surrounded by some of the tallest mountains on Earth, with freezing temperatures, powerful winds and barely half the
articles.body: Imagine flying over the Himalayas, surrounded by some of the tallest mountains on Earth, with freezing temperatures, powerful winds and barely half the oxygen available at sea level. Now imagine doing it without an oxygen cylinder, specialised climbing equipment or even a place to stop and catch your breath!For the bar-headed goose, this is not an extreme adventure; in fact, for them, it’s a biannual journey that has fascinated scientists for decades. This goose isn’t dodging traffic or bad weather; it’s pushing through ice-cold winds, fighting for breath in air that holds only a fraction of the oxygen found at sea level, and soaring at altitudes where even experienced mountaineers fear to tread. And it does it all using nothing but its own wings and some clever evolutionary tricks.As Smithsonian Mag points out, every autumn and spring, these geese (Anser indicus) move between their winter homes in the Indian subcontinent and their breeding grounds across Central Asia, including the Tibetan Plateau and Mongolia, and travel south to the Indian subcontinent during winter. They cross the Himalayas, flying over harsh terrain, almost always at night or in the early hours of the day. It’s not drama or legend: researchers have tracked them with satellite transmitters and mapped their unlikely routes.But what’s really amazing is how these geese do what would kill most others. They don't stop for extra oxygen, wrap up in specialized gear, or look for rest stops. The plain fact is, a bar-headed goose’s body is a high-altitude machine — one that’s tuned for survival in the thinnest air on Earth.What makes the bar-headed goose so special?If you’ve ever seen one, the bar-headed goose stands out with its white plumage and signature pair of dark bars stretching across the back of its head. But it’s not the markings that intrigue scientists; it’s what’s going on inside. This bird’s annual migration is an all-out test of endurance and adaptation.A study published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) tracked the birds using satellite transmitters. Researchers discovered that rather than waiting for the warmest, calmest days, most geese make their Himalayan crossing precisely when conditions are toughest: at night or before sunrise, often when winds are relatively still. And their climbs are remarkable. In spring, they can ascend thousands of metres; sometimes jumping from 4,000 to over 6,000 metres in a matter of hours. On the way back south, their trips can be shorter, but the challenge is the same.Surviving on half the oxygenAt the altitudes these geese tackle (5,000 metres and higher), the air is so thin that even breathing feels like a workout. Try jogging at that height, and you’ll struggle. Yet, the bar-headed goose can fly for hours nonstop.How? It’s all in the genes and the body's design:Supercharged hemoglobin: The blood of these geese carries oxygen more efficiently than that of other birds. Their hemoglobin holds a stronger grip on oxygen, pulling it from the scarce air and shuttling it quickly to where it’s needed most: muscles burning fuel as the bird flaps its wings.Bigger and smarter lungs: Unlike their lowland cousins, bar-headed geese have powerful lungs that expand more and breathe in greater amounts of air. When the going gets tough, they simply breathe harder and deeper, making every breath count.Oxygen-soaked muscles: Their flight muscles have an incredible network of tiny blood vessels, called capillaries. More capillaries mean that oxygen flows faster and more generously into muscle cells, keeping those wings moving even in near-starvation conditions.Smarter flying over flexing strengthIt’s tempting to think the bar-headed goose just powers over the mountain range like a jetliner. But in reality, it’s even more clever than that. Studies, including a big one published in Science in 2015, show that these geese use a “roller coaster” approach. They don’t always aim for the highest possible path. Instead, they ride up and down with the landscape, skirting along valleys, dipping when the ground drops, and only climbing when there’s no other choice. Sometimes, they use rising air currents near mountain slopes to lift themselves higher with less work.This route, though longer or less direct, makes a huge difference, because flying higher takes more effort as air gets thinner. Saving energy is crucial; it means more birds survive the crossing.Do these geese really fly over Mt. Everest?There’s a popular image of these geese: silhouetted against snow, gliding just above Everest’s peak. But the facts paint a slightly different, though no less impressive, picture. According to the United States Geological Survey, tracking has shown that almost all geese avoid the very highest summits, sticking to valleys and lower passes. On record, some have hit altitudes above 7,000 metres, but most of their journey is spent below 5,500 metres. Still, few living creatures (human or animal) ever reach those heights under their own power.Why is this journey so special?The bar-headed goose is a living, flapping, honking lesson in adaptation. It’s not brute strength or luck, but countless subtle biological upgrades like better hemoglobin, bigger lungs, and muscle tweaks that allow it to do the impossible. And then there’s instinct: the knowledge to zigzag through deadly mountain weather, ride air currents, and pick the perfect time to go. To the scientists who track these migrations and poke through goose DNA, these birds are not merely extraordinary adventures; they’re an endless source of clues about how life can adapt to extreme conditions.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates.
